title: Introduce WHO-recommended vaccines against childhood malaria

concept.text: Prevent clinical malaria in children through vaccines suitable for endemic-country immunization programmes. RTS,S and R21 achieved WHO recommendation, although neither completes the existing 90%-efficacy target. Proposed completion test: WHO recommendation for routine childhood use in endemic settings, based on clinical efficacy, safety and public-health benefit, followed by WHO prequalification for international procurement. Test set by: WHO, advised by SAGE and the Malaria Policy Advisory Group. Reported achieved: WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 on 6 October 2021 and R21/Matrix-M on 2 October 2023; both subsequently obtained WHO prequalification. Overlaps: INF-13. Sources given: [WHO RTS,S recommendation](https://www.who.int/News/Item/06-10-2021-Who-Recommends-Groundbreaking-Malaria-Vaccine-for-Children-at-Risk) ; [WHO R21 recommendation](https://www.who.int/news/item/02-10-2023-who-recommends-r21-matrix-m-vaccine-for-malaria-prevention-in-updated-advice-on-immunization) ; [WHO malaria vaccine questions and answers](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/q-a-on-rts-s-malaria-vaccine).

page.title: WHO-recommended and prequalified childhood malaria vaccines
page.definition: Vaccines against Plasmodium falciparum, a malaria-causing parasite, are recommended by WHO for children in endemic areas and prequalified for procurement by United Nations agencies. RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M meet these conditions.

goal.need: An estimated 438,000 African children died of malaria in 2024. In high-transmission areas, young children can have four to six episodes a year even with insecticide-treated nets and access to diagnosis and treatment. Vaccination adds protection and can reach children who do not sleep under a net. In Ghana, Kenya and Malawi, areas that introduced RTS,S had 13% lower mortality from causes other than injury among children old enough for three doses than areas awaiting introduction.

figures.caption: WHO estimates of the malaria burden in 2024
figures.note: The childhood deaths are included in the worldwide death total.

statements.quote: The vaccine should reduce the incidence of all clinical malaria episodes.
statements.context: Preferred product characteristics for vaccines to reduce malaria morbidity and mortality.

statements.body: Malaria Vaccine Technology Roadmap Working Group
statements.quote: a protective efficacy of more than 50% against severe disease and death and lasts longer than one year
statements.context: The roadmap set this efficacy and duration target for development and licensure of a first-generation malaria vaccine by 2015. WHO’s later recommendation and prequalification are separate decisions.

completion.title: WHO recommends a malaria vaccine for children in endemic areas and prequalifies it.
completion.criterion: WHO recommends the vaccine for programmatic prevention of P. falciparum malaria in children living in malaria-endemic areas, prioritizing moderate and high transmission, and lists the same product as prequalified for United Nations procurement. Completion is the later of the recommendation date and the effective date of prequalification.
completion.set_by: World Health Organization, through its malaria vaccine policy recommendation and vaccine prequalification programme.
completion.threshold_quote: Two malaria vaccines, RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M, are WHO-prequalified and recommended for use.
completion.basis: WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 for wider childhood use on 6 October 2021 after evaluating pilot introductions in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi. Its prequalification took effect on 15 July 2022. WHO recommended R21/Matrix-M on 2 October 2023. Its prequalification took effect on 19 December 2023 and was announced on 21 December. Prequalification is required for UNICEF procurement and Gavi funding for deployment.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine reduces infection after human challenge at two-sided p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Show that a smaller proportion of vaccinated adults than unvaccinated controls develop microscopy-detected P. falciparum infection after controlled human challenge. In the phase 2a protocol NCT01857869, follow-up extends through day 28 after challenge and the comparison uses a two-sided Fisher exact test at p<0.05.
milestones.set_by: Regules et al., RTS,S/AS01 phase 2a protocol NCT01857869; this statistical test and follow-up period were specified for that study.
milestones.threshold_quote: All statistical tests were 2-tailed at 5% significance level.

milestones.title: A phase 2 field trial shows protection against clinical malaria in children at p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Show positive efficacy against a prespecified clinical malaria endpoint in a randomized phase 2 field trial in children, at the trial’s 5% significance level. In NCT00380393 the primary analysis compared time to the first episode in the per-protocol groups. A case required an axillary temperature of at least 37.5°C and more than 2,500 P. falciparum parasites per microlitre.
milestones.set_by: Bejon et al., randomized phase 2b trial NCT00380393.

milestones.title: A malaria vaccine reduces clinical-malaria episodes in a phase 3 trial at p<0.05.
milestones.criterion: Show fewer episodes of clinical P. falciparum malaria in vaccinated children than in controls in a randomized phase 3 field trial. Compare the groups over the prespecified follow-up period using the trial’s clinical case definition. The RTS,S final analysis used p<0.05.
milestones.set_by: RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, NCT00866619 final-analysis plan; the quoted significance threshold was specified for that analysis.
milestones.threshold_quote: p values less than 0·05 were deemed significant.

milestones.title: A childhood malaria vaccine receives a positive regulatory benefit–risk assessment.
milestones.criterion: Obtain a positive regulatory assessment of the vaccine’s quality, safety and efficacy for its intended childhood indication. Under the European Medicines Agency’s Article 58 route for use outside the European Union, the decision takes the form of a positive scientific opinion that the benefits outweigh the risks.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Article 58 assessment of Mosquirix; this assessment route was used for RTS,S/AS01.
milestones.threshold_quote: The Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) therefore concluded that the benefits of the vaccine outweigh its risks

milestones.title: RTS,S pilot data resolve the safety signals and show trends consistent with clinical benefit.
milestones.criterion: In routine childhood use of RTS,S/AS01, resolve the phase 3 signals for meningitis, cerebral malaria and sex-specific mortality by excluding risks of important size or establishing a positive benefit–risk profile despite adverse events. Trends in severe malaria or mortality must also be consistent with benefit. The initial policy review uses accrued pilot data on safety and impact.
milestones.set_by: WHO SAGE and Malaria Policy Advisory Committee, 2019 framework for policy decision on RTS,S/AS01; this pilot requirement was written for RTS,S/AS01.
milestones.threshold_quote: concerns regarding the safety signals observed in the Phase 3 trial (related to meningitis, cerebral malaria and sex-specific mortality) are satisfactorily resolved

milestones.title: WHO recommends a malaria vaccine for childhood use in endemic areas.
milestones.criterion: WHO publishes a recommendation for programmatic use of the vaccine to prevent P. falciparum malaria in children living in endemic areas, with priority given to areas of moderate and high transmission.
milestones.set_by: World Health Organization, following advice from the Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization and the Malaria Policy Advisory Group.
milestones.threshold_quote: WHO recommends the use of malaria vaccines for the prevention of P. falciparum malaria in children living in malaria endemic areas

milestones.title: A phase 1 study establishes initial safety and an immune response in healthy adults.
milestones.criterion: Assess adverse events and the immune response to the candidate vaccine in healthy adults. For a recombinant malaria vaccine, measure antibody concentrations to the vaccine antigen with a validated assay. WHO calls for adult data from people with and without prior malaria exposure when the intended recipients are children.
milestones.set_by: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization, Technical Report Series 980, Annex 3, Part C.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial safety and immunogenicity studies in healthy adults – i.e. phase I studies

milestones.title: Animal studies support a malaria vaccine candidate’s potential to protect against disease.
milestones.criterion: Show that the candidate induces an immune response to the vaccine antigen in animals. Where a suitable protection model exists, assess protection as well. The findings must support a reasonable expectation of protection against clinical malaria.
milestones.set_by: WHO Expert Committee on Biological Standardization, Technical Report Series 980, Annex 3, Part B.
milestones.threshold_quote: reasonably likely, on the basis of animal immunogenicity and, when applicable, protection data, to provide protection from clinical malaria.

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01E showed 53% adjusted efficacy against a first episode of clinical malaria in 809 per-protocol children.
results.quote: the adjusted efficacy rate for RTS,S/AS01E was 53% (95% confidence interval [CI], 28 to 69; P<0.001) on the basis of Cox regression.

results.finding: R21/Matrix-M with 50 μg adjuvant showed 77% efficacy against first clinical malaria episodes through 6 months in the primary analysis of 439 children.
results.detail: In NCT03896724 the primary case definition required an axillary temperature of at least 37.5°C and more than 5,000 asexual P. falciparum parasites per μL.
results.quote: Vaccine efficacy was 74% (95% CI 63–82) in group 1 and 77% (67–84) in group 2 at 6 months.

results.finding: Among 8,922 children in the phase 3 analysis, RTS,S/AS01 with a booster had 36.3% efficacy against clinical malaria episodes.
results.detail: The primary case definition required illness with axillary temperature ≥37.5°C and >5,000 asexual P. falciparum parasites per µL, or a case meeting the primary severe-malaria definition.
results.quote:

clinical malaria that met the primary case definition in children in the C3C
group, 6616 episodes occurred in the R3R group (VE 36·3%, 95% CI
31·8–40·5)

results.finding: R21/Matrix-M showed 72% efficacy against all clinical malaria episodes in 4,643 children in the pooled phase 3 analysis.
results.detail: The modified per-protocol cohort included 4,644 children. Table 2 reports 4,643 in the pooled clinical-malaria comparison.
results.quote: Across all sites, vaccine efficacy against multiple episodes of malaria was 72% (69–75; p<0·0001;

results.finding: EMA’s CHMP issued a positive scientific opinion for Mosquirix on 23 July 2015.
results.detail: The main efficacy study informing the assessment enrolled over 12,000 children in seven African countries.
results.quote: The Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) therefore concluded that the benefits of the vaccine outweigh its risks and issued a positive scientific opinion.

results.finding: In the 158-cluster RTS,S pilot, severe malaria admissions fell by 32% among children eligible for three doses.
results.detail: The initial analysis covered about 24 months in Ghana and Malawi and 19 months in Kenya. Cerebral malaria monitoring continued because the confidence interval still allowed the expected phase 3 signal after dilution.
results.quote: Among children eligible for RTS,S-3, there was a 32% reduction in hospital admissions with severe malaria (427 in the intervention areas and 697 from comparison areas; IRR 0·68 [95% CI 0·49–0·95]).

results.finding: Across 158 clusters, routine RTS,S introduction was associated with a mortality rate ratio of 0·87 among children eligible for three doses.
results.detail: The 46-month analysis followed the initial WHO policy review. The girls-to-boys ratio of mortality rate ratios was 1·00 (95% CI 0·90–1·12). Earlier pilot data had excluded a sex interaction as large as the one observed in phase 3.
results.quote:
The mortality rate 
ratio was 0·87 (95% CI 0·77–0·97; p=0·016).

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01 pilots in three countries found no association with any of the 3 phase 3 safety signals. The summary gives no participant count.
results.detail: The summary reports significance for both clinical outcomes without giving effect sizes or p-values. It does not identify which data cutoff informed the initial policy review.
results.quote:
The safety signals were not found to be associated with vaccination, supporting the 
conclusion that they were chance findings.

results.finding: WHO recommends 2 malaria vaccines for children in endemic areas, prioritizing moderate and high transmission.
results.quote:
WHO recommends the use of malaria vaccines for the prevention of P. falciparum malaria in 
children living in malaria endemic areas, prioritizing areas of moderate and high transmission.

results.finding: WHO lists 2 childhood malaria vaccines as both recommended and prequalified by May 2024.
results.quote:
Two malaria vaccines, RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M, are WHO-prequalified and recommended 
for use.

results.finding: WHO announced prequalification of R21/Matrix-M on 21 December 2023. No study sample applies.
results.detail: The release states no separate effective date, so the announcement date is used for completion.
results.quote: Today marks a huge stride in global health as we welcome the prequalification of R21/Matrix-M, the second malaria vaccine recommended for children in malaria endemic areas.

results.finding: Among 6,861 children originally recruited, adding RTS,S/AS01E to seasonal malaria chemoprevention gave 57.7% efficacy against clinical malaria versus chemoprevention alone.
results.detail: The superiority comparison estimates the benefit of adding RTS,S/AS01E to seasonal malaria chemoprevention. RTS,S/AS01E alone met the non-inferiority margin against chemoprevention alone.
results.quote:
Protective efficacy 
in the combined group was 57· 7% (95% CI 53· 3−61·7) 
compared with SMC alone and 59· 0% (54· 7−62·8) 
compared with RTS,S/AS01E-alone.

results.finding: In a phase 3 trial that recruited 6,861 children, zero suspected meningitis cases were confirmed.
results.detail: The pooled vaccine groups versus SMC alone had a sex-by-treatment mortality interaction estimate of 1.01 (95% CI 0.38–2.68) for deaths excluding external causes and surgery.
results.quote:
Ten possible cases of meningitis were 
investigated by lumbar puncture, eight during the first 
3 years of the study, and two during the extension period. 
Cerebrospinal fluid examination excluded a diagnosis of 
meningitis in all of these children.

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01E showed 53% adjusted efficacy against a first clinical malaria episode in 809 children analyzed per protocol.
results.detail: Per-protocol follow-up began 2 weeks after the final vaccination and averaged 8 months.
results.quote:
the adjusted efficacy rate for RTS,S/AS01E was 53% (95% 
confidence interval [CI], 28 to 69; P<0.001) on the basis of Cox regression.

results.finding: R21/Matrix-M provided sterile protection in 7 of 8 BALB/c mice in each challenge.
results.detail: Sterile protection was defined as no parasites detected by day 14 after challenge. Adjuvant-only controls showed no protection.
results.quote:
87.5% with R21+  Matrix M (7/8 p =  0.0002, 
and 7/8 p <  0.0001 in a second independent challenge) (Fig. 5a).

results.finding: In malaria-naive adults (104 RTS,S/AS01 recipients and 24 unvaccinated controls), microscopy-confirmed infection after challenge was 47.5 percentage points lower among vaccine recipients.
results.detail: Challenge took place 3 months after the final vaccination. The reported 24-control denominator includes two participants who withdrew before day 28 and received presumptive treatment. Both were smear-negative at withdrawal and were excluded from the per-protocol efficacy analysis.
results.quote: After CHMI at 3 months after the last vaccination, 22 of 24 infectivity controls (91.7%), and 46 of 104 vaccinated participants(44.2%) presented with confirmed  P. falciparum  infection.

results.finding: Among 409 children who received a booster, high-dose R21/Matrix-M showed 80% efficacy against a first episode of clinical malaria over the next year.
results.detail: The efficacy population required completion of the primary series and receipt of a booster. The high-dose comparison involved 137 vaccine recipients and 140 controls.
results.quote: Vaccine efficacy was 71% (95% CI 60 to 78) in the low-dose adjuvant group and 80% (72 to 85) in the high-dose adjuvant group.

results.finding: RTS,S/AS01E regimens reduced clinical malaria episodes versus rabies vaccine in the exposed set of 1,500 children (nominal p<0.001 for each regimen).
results.detail: The 50-month vaccine-versus-control comparisons were secondary. The trial’s primary objective tested whether a fractional third dose was superior to a full third dose, and superiority was not demonstrated.
results.quote: Among children in the exposed set, to month 50, vaccine efficacy against all episodes of clinical malaria was 36% (95% CI 19–50), 51% (37–61), 43% (28–55), and 41% (26–53) in groups R012-20, R012-14-26-38, Fx012-14-26-38, and Fx017-20-32, respectively (p<0·001 for all).

results.finding: NAFDAC found a favorable benefit–risk balance for R21/Matrix-M in children aged 5–36 months. The briefing gives no trial sample size.
results.detail: NAFDAC communicated the need for a phase 4 clinical trial or pharmacovigilance study in Nigeria when granting provisional approval.
results.quote: The Joint Review Committee concluded that the data on the R21 Malaria vaccine were robust and met criteria for efficacy, safety, and quality. It was also adjudged that the vaccine’s known and potential benefits outweigh its known and potential risks, thereby supporting the manufacturer’s recommended use.

results.finding: Routine RTS,S/AS01 use in Ghana, Kenya and Malawi (182 cerebral malaria cases, 727 controls recruited) showed 61% effectiveness against cerebral malaria.
results.detail: The cerebral malaria estimate compared any dose with no doses. Documented vaccination histories were available for 146 cases and 539 controls. The estimate comes from the later case–control analysis reviewed by the DSMB and working group.
results.quote:
Compared to receiving no doses of RTS,S/AS01, receiving one or more doses of RTS,S/AS01 was associated 
with an average protective effectiveness of 61% (95% CI: 35–76%) against cerebral malaria (Table 5).

results.finding: WHO recommends RTS,S/AS01 for children in areas with moderate to high P. falciparum transmission, based on a pilot that reached more than 900,000 children.
results.quote:
WHO recommends that in the context of comprehensive malaria control the RTS,S/AS01 malaria vaccine be used for the prevention of
P. falciparum
malaria in children living in regions with moderate to high transmission as defined by WHO.
